# Copy structure

The structural conventions for the copy kind — a standalone piece read start to finish. A prose ADR for a piece or a set of pieces selects from these shapes and binds them as rules; the piece's writer complies.

## Argument arc

Arguments progress. Each paragraph moves the piece forward — developing, supporting, or transitioning. A paragraph that could swap places with an earlier one without the reader noticing is redundant. The arc — what the piece opens with, what it builds through, where it lands — is the piece's structure.

## Example economy

One developed example beats a stack. An example with real detail carries an argument; four examples at a sentence each substitute name-dropping for analysis. Develop each example that adds distinct information; cut the rest.

## Device budget

Rhetorical devices are single-use. One metaphor introduced, used, and released. One rule-of-three at the moment of payoff. A device that returns asks the reader to admire the writing instead of following the argument.

## Length

Length matches substance. A piece with one core insight is short. Word count tracks new information and reasoning, not the thesis's importance. A draft restating its core point more than twice is too long.

## Endings

Endings end. The piece stops when the last new idea is complete — no summary ritual, no announced conclusion.

## Tradeoffs

Tradeoffs live in place. Real difficulties appear in the section where they are relevant, with the same specificity and sourcing as any other claim — never as a bookend concession.
